28Properties that save work

Linearity lets you transform term by term, a shift of kkk samples multiplies by z−kz^{-k}z−k, and convolution becomes multiplication.

PropertySequencez-transformROC
Linearityαx(n)+βy(n)\alpha x(n) + \beta y(n)αx(n)+βy(n)αX(z)+βY(z)\alpha X(z) + \beta Y(z)αX(z)+βY(z)includes Rx∩RyR_x \cap R_yRx​∩Ry​
Time shiftx(n−k)x(n-k)x(n−k)z−kX(z)z^{-k}X(z)z−kX(z)RxR_xRx​, except possibly z=0z = 0z=0 or ∞\infty∞
Convolutionx(n)∗y(n)x(n) * y(n)x(n)∗y(n)X(z) Y(z)X(z)\,Y(z)X(z)Y(z)includes Rx∩RyR_x \cap R_yRx​∩Ry​
Time reversalx(−n)x(-n)x(−n)X(1/z)X(1/z)X(1/z)1/Rx1/R_x1/Rx​
Conjugationx∗(n)x^*(n)x∗(n)X∗(z∗)X^*(z^*)X∗(z∗)RxR_xRx​
  • Linearity is what made example 3 easy: transform each part, add, and keep the zzz where both converge.
  • Time shift is the reason a difference equation turns into algebra: every y(n−k)y(n-k)y(n−k) becomes z−kY(z)z^{-k}Y(z)z−kY(z). The next lectures use this to get H(z)H(z)H(z) from any difference equation (slides 24–25).
  • Convolution becoming multiplication is the main reason signal engineers like the z-transform, just as with the DTFT (section 10) and the Laplace transform. For an LTI system, Y(z)=H(z)X(z)Y(z) = H(z)X(z)Y(z)=H(z)X(z).
  • Time reversal flips the sequence about n=0n = 0n=0 and turns the ROC inside out: ∣z∣>r|z| \gt r∣z∣>r becomes ∣z∣<1/r|z| \lt 1/r∣z∣<1/r. (In the recording it comes out sounding like a shift; the slide has it right.)

29Poles, zeros and the pole-zero plot

Write X(z)X(z)X(z) as a ratio of polynomials. The roots of the top are zeros, the roots of the bottom are poles, and once those at 000 and ∞\infty∞ are counted there are as many of one as of the other.

X(z)=N(z)D(z)=b0+b1z−1+⋯+bMz−Ma0+a1z−1+⋯+aNz−N=b0a0 zN−M (z−z1)(z−z2)⋯(z−zM)(z−p1)(z−p2)⋯(z−pN).X(z) = \frac{N(z)}{D(z)} = \frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + \cdots + b_M z^{-M}}{a_0 + a_1 z^{-1} + \cdots + a_N z^{-N}} = \frac{b_0}{a_0}\,z^{N-M}\,\frac{(z - z_1)(z - z_2)\cdots(z - z_M)}{(z - p_1)(z - p_2)\cdots(z - p_N)}.X(z)=D(z)N(z)​=a0​+a1​z−1+⋯+aN​z−Nb0​+b1​z−1+⋯+bM​z−M​=a0​b0​​zN−M(z−p1​)(z−p2​)⋯(z−pN​)(z−z1​)(z−z2​)⋯(z−zM​)​.

Multiplying top and bottom by the highest power of zzz is the “massaging” the lecture kept doing: exam questions rarely hand you X(z)X(z)X(z) already factorised. Then (slide 21):

  • MMM finite zeros z1,…,zMz_1, \dots, z_Mz1​,…,zM​ and NNN finite poles p1,…,pNp_1, \dots, p_Np1​,…,pN​;
  • ∣N−M∣|N - M|∣N−M∣ extra zeros at the origin if N>MN \gt MN>M, or extra poles at the origin if N<MN \lt MN<M;
  • a zero at z=∞z = \inftyz=∞ if X(∞)=0X(\infty) = 0X(∞)=0, a pole there if X(∞)=∞X(\infty) = \inftyX(∞)=∞;
  • so, counted this way, the numbers of poles and zeros are equal.

The pole-zero plot (slides 22–23)

Draw the pole-zero plot and ROC of x(n)=(12)nu(n)+(−13)nu(n)x(n) = (\tfrac12)^n u(n) + (-\tfrac13)^n u(n)x(n)=(21​)nu(n)+(−31​)nu(n). Both terms are causal:

X(z)=11−12z−1+11+13z−1=2z (z−112)(z−12)(z+13),∣z∣>12.X(z) = \frac{1}{1 - \tfrac12 z^{-1}} + \frac{1}{1 + \tfrac13 z^{-1}} = \frac{2z\,\big(z - \tfrac{1}{12}\big)}{\big(z - \tfrac12\big)\big(z + \tfrac13\big)}, \qquad |z| \gt \tfrac12.X(z)=1−21​z−11​+1+31​z−11​=(z−21​)(z+31​)2z(z−121​)​,∣z∣>21​.

Everything is on the real axis because the poles are real. The ROC starts at the largest pole, 12\tfrac1221​, because the sequence is causal; and it contains the unit circle, so the system is stable. The lecture: “I can tell that immediately from the diagram.”

A pole-zero plot from Assignment 1

The example notebook Bandstop_ECG.ipynb removes 50 Hz mains from an ECG sampled at 250 Hz with a second-order IIR notch:

HBS(z)=1+α2⋅1−2cos⁡ω0 z−1+z−21−(1+α)cos⁡ω0 z−1+αz−2,ω0=2π⋅50250=0.4π,α=0.97517788.H_{BS}(z) = \frac{1+\alpha}{2}\cdot\frac{1 - 2\cos\omega_0\,z^{-1} + z^{-2}}{1 - (1+\alpha)\cos\omega_0\,z^{-1} + \alpha z^{-2}}, \qquad \omega_0 = 2\pi\cdot\tfrac{50}{250} = 0.4\pi,\quad \alpha = 0.97517788.HBS​(z)=21+α​⋅1−(1+α)cosω0​z−1+αz−21−2cosω0​z−1+z−2​,ω0​=2π⋅25050​=0.4π,α=0.97517788.

The numerator factorises as (1−ejω0z−1)(1−e−jω0z−1)(1 - e^{j\omega_0}z^{-1})(1 - e^{-j\omega_0}z^{-1})(1−ejω0​z−1)(1−e−jω0​z−1), so the zeros are e±j0.4πe^{\pm j0.4\pi}e±j0.4π, exactly on the unit circle at the 50 Hz angle. The denominator's roots are 0.9875 e±j0.4π0.9875\,e^{\pm j0.4\pi}0.9875e±j0.4π: two poles just inside the circle, right behind the zeros. Both poles are inside the unit circle, so the causal filter is stable.

A zero on the unit circle at 50 Hz blocks that frequency completely; the pole just behind it keeps the notch narrow (a 1 Hz 3 dB bandwidth here). Why a nearby pole narrows the notch is slides 45–47, still to come.

30Getting x(n) back: the inverse z-transform

Factor the denominator, expand X(z)/zX(z)/zX(z)/z in partial fractions, match each term to the table, and use the ROC to decide which terms are causal and which anti-causal.

Slide 11 lists three methods: the Cauchy inversion formula (a contour integral), power series (long division), and partial fractions. The lecture used partial fractions, with the cover-up method; it is worth revising if it has gone rusty.

The recipe (slides 12–13)

  1. Clear the negative powers and factorise the denominator to find the poles pkp_kpk​.
  2. Divide by zzz and expand X(z)z=∑kCkz−pk\dfrac{X(z)}{z} = \sum_k \dfrac{C_k}{z - p_k}zX(z)​=∑k​z−pk​Ck​​, with Ck=[(z−pk)X(z)z]z=pkC_k = \Big[(z - p_k)\dfrac{X(z)}{z}\Big]_{z = p_k}Ck​=[(z−pk​)zX(z)​]z=pk​​ (cover up the factor, substitute the pole).
  3. Multiply back by zzz: X(z)=∑kCkzz−pkX(z) = \sum_k C_k\dfrac{z}{z - p_k}X(z)=∑k​Ck​z−pk​z​. Each term is row 4 or row 6 of the table.
  4. Use the ROC: a pole inside the ROC's inner edge gives a causal term Ckpknu(n)C_k p_k^n u(n)Ck​pkn​u(n); a pole outside its outer edge gives an anti-causal term −Ckpknu(−n−1)-C_k p_k^n u(-n-1)−Ck​pkn​u(−n−1).

Dividing by zzz first is what makes every term come out as zz−p\dfrac{z}{z - p}z−pz​, the form in the table. (If the numerator and denominator have the same degree in z−1z^{-1}z−1, a constant B0B_0B0​ appears as well, slide 13; the examples here don't need one.)

Slide 14: find x(n)x(n)x(n) for X(z)=z−11−0.25z−1−0.375z−2X(z) = \dfrac{z^{-1}}{1 - 0.25z^{-1} - 0.375z^{-2}}X(z)=1−0.25z−1−0.375z−2z−1​, ROC ∣z∣>0.75|z| \gt 0.75∣z∣>0.75

C1=1z+0.5∣z=0.75=11.25=45,C2=1z−0.75∣z=−0.5=1−1.25=−45.C_1 = \frac{1}{z + 0.5}\bigg|_{z = 0.75} = \frac{1}{1.25} = \frac45, \qquad C_2 = \frac{1}{z - 0.75}\bigg|_{z = -0.5} = \frac{1}{-1.25} = -\frac45.C1​=z+0.51​​z=0.75​=1.251​=54​,C2​=z−0.751​​z=−0.5​=−1.251​=−54​.

The ROC ∣z∣>0.75|z| \gt 0.75∣z∣>0.75 is outside the largest pole, so both terms are causal. A check by long division: X(z)=z−1+0.25z−2+⋯X(z) = z^{-1} + 0.25z^{-2} + \cdotsX(z)=z−1+0.25z−2+⋯, so x(0)=0x(0) = 0x(0)=0, x(1)=1x(1) = 1x(1)=1, x(2)=0.25x(2) = 0.25x(2)=0.25, and the formula gives the same.

The board: X(z)=−3z2z2−5z+2X(z) = \dfrac{-3z}{2z^2 - 5z + 2}X(z)=2z2−5z+2−3z​, ROC contains the unit circle

2z2−5z+2=(2z−1)(z−2)2z^2 - 5z + 2 = (2z - 1)(z - 2)2z2−5z+2=(2z−1)(z−2), so the poles are 12\tfrac1221​ and 222. The first expansion the lecture wrote wasn't in table form; with the recipe above it is

An ROC that contains ∣z∣=1|z| = 1∣z∣=1, with poles at 12\tfrac1221​ and 2, can only be the ring 12<∣z∣<2\tfrac12 \lt |z| \lt 221​<∣z∣<2. The pole at 12\tfrac1221​ is inside it, a causal term; the pole at 2 is outside it, an anti-causal term (row 6, which is where the minus signs cancel):

x(n)=(12)nu(n)+2nu(−n−1).x(n) = \Big(\tfrac12\Big)^n u(n) + 2^n u(-n-1).x(n)=(21​)nu(n)+2nu(−n−1).

Both halves shrink away from n=0n = 0n=0: 12,14,…\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots21​,41​,… to the right and 12,14,…\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots21​,41​,… to the left. So even with an anti-causal part the sum converges and the system is stable, as a ring containing the unit circle promises.

Lectures 5–6Slides 32–36, previewed in both lectures

31Stability: does the ROC contain the unit circle?

A system is BIBO stable exactly when its ROC contains the unit circle. For a causal system that means every pole lies inside the unit circle.

BIBO stability needs ∑∣h(n)∣<∞\sum |h(n)| \lt \infty∑∣h(n)∣<∞ (section 8). On the unit circle ∣z−n∣=1|z^{-n}| = 1∣z−n∣=1, so

∣H(z)∣∣∣z∣=1≤∑n∣h(n)∣ ∣z−n∣=∑n∣h(n)∣.|H(z)|\Big|_{|z| = 1} \le \sum_n |h(n)|\,|z^{-n}| = \sum_n |h(n)|.∣H(z)∣​∣z∣=1​≤n∑​∣h(n)∣∣z−n∣=n∑​∣h(n)∣.

If hhh is absolutely summable, the sum converges on the unit circle, which puts the unit circle in the ROC (slides 32–33). For a causal system the ROC is ∣z∣>|z| \gt∣z∣> the largest pole, so it contains ∣z∣=1|z| = 1∣z∣=1 exactly when every pole is inside the unit circle.

  • (78)nu(n)(\tfrac78)^n u(n)(87​)nu(n): pole at 78\tfrac7887​, inside. Stable.
  • The Fibonacci system of section 21: H(z)=11−z−1−z−2=z2z2−z−1H(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 - z^{-1} - z^{-2}} = \dfrac{z^2}{z^2 - z - 1}H(z)=1−z−1−z−21​=z2−z−1z2​, poles at 1±52=1.618\tfrac{1 \pm \sqrt5}{2} = 1.61821±5​​=1.618 and −0.618-0.618−0.618. The causal ROC ∣z∣>1.618|z| \gt 1.618∣z∣>1.618 misses the unit circle: unstable, hence 1,1,2,3,5,8,…1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots1,1,2,3,5,8,… The pole at 1.618 is the golden ratio, which is why each term is about 1.618 times the last.
  • The board example (poles 12\tfrac1221​ and 2): stable, because its ring contains the circle, but not causal.
  • Poles on the circle, as in Q21.1 (e±jπ/3e^{\pm j\pi/3}e±jπ/3) or u(n)u(n)u(n) (a pole at 1): the output neither grows nor dies away, ∑∣h(n)∣\sum|h(n)|∑∣h(n)∣ diverges, and the system is not BIBO stable.

Two slips in the 22 September recording

  • “For stable systems, we require the region of convergence to be located inside the unit circle.” It is the poles that must be inside, for a causal system. The ROC must contain the unit circle (slide 33), and the lecture goes on to say exactly that.
  • An unstable system is described as having an ROC “that extends to infinity”. Every causal ROC extends to infinity. What decides stability is whether it reaches in as far as ∣z∣=1|z| = 1∣z∣=1.

ReviseMistakes the lectures warned about

Common traps

Part 1 · LTI systems

  • Impulse vs impulse response. δ(n)\delta(n)δ(n) is the input; h(n)h(n)h(n) is what the system gives back.
  • The star. x∗hx * hx∗h is convolution, not multiplication, and convolution is not a sample-by-sample operation.
  • Shift direction. x(n−2)x(n-2)x(n−2) is xxx moved right (later), not left.
  • Offsets. y(n)=x(n)+1y(n) = x(n) + 1y(n)=x(n)+1 is not linear: zero in must give zero out.
  • Bounded isn't stable. A bounded h(n)h(n)h(n) can still fail ∑∣h(n)∣<∞\sum|h(n)| \lt \infty∑∣h(n)∣<∞; the ideal filter's sinc does.
  • Which FIR filters have linear phase. Only symmetric ones.
  • Angle vs delay. The same phase angle at every frequency is not the same time delay.
  • Taps vs order. 8 taps is 7th order; 101 taps is order 100.
  • Difference-equation conventions. Check the sign on a(k)a(k)a(k) and where each sum starts.
  • Phase jumps. Jumps of π\piπ in a linear-phase plot are sign flips of A(ω)A(\omega)A(ω), not non-linearity.
  • “Nyquist frequency”. Here it means 2Fmax⁡2F_{\max}2Fmax​; many books call that the Nyquist rate.
  • The DTFT sign. It is e−jωne^{-j\omega n}e−jωn; slides 27 and 29 print a plus sign.
  • sin⁡(πn)=0\sin(\pi n) = 0sin(πn)=0. It vanishes for every whole-number nnn. The band-stop derivation (2023, Q1) needs this step.
  • Negative symmetry means sines. The pairs become 2jsin⁡2j\sin2jsin, and that jjj is where β=π/2\beta = \pi/2β=π/2 comes from.

Part 2 · The z-transform

  • An X(z)X(z)X(z) on its own is not an answer. Rows 4 and 6 of the table share zz−a\frac{z}{z - a}z−az​; only the ROC says which signal you mean, so always state it.
  • “ROC inside the unit circle” is not stability. The ROC must contain the unit circle. For a causal system it is the poles that sit inside it.
  • Divide by zzz first. Expanding X(z)X(z)X(z) itself leaves terms like 1z−p\frac{1}{z - p}z−p1​, which are not in the table. Expanding X(z)/zX(z)/zX(z)/z gives zz−p\frac{z}{z - p}z−pz​, which is.
  • Negative powers hide poles and zeros. 11−az−1\frac{1}{1 - az^{-1}}1−az−11​ seems to have no zero, but zz−a\frac{z}{z - a}z−az​ has one at the origin. Multiply through by the highest power of zzz before reading them off.
  • u(−n−1)u(-n-1)u(−n−1) stops at n=−1n = -1n=−1. The anti-causal pair has no sample at n=0n = 0n=0, and row 6 carries a minus sign: it is −anu(−n−1)-a^n u(-n-1)−anu(−n−1), not anu(−n−1)a^n u(-n-1)anu(−n−1).
  • z+1z^{+1}z+1 is an advance. A positive power of zzz shifts a sequence to the left, earlier in time. A delay is z−1z^{-1}z−1.
  • Z-Transform slide 3, row 9. The denominator of ansin⁡(ω0n) u(n)a^n\sin(\omega_0 n)\,u(n)ansin(ω0​n)u(n) has cos⁡ω0\cos\omega_0cosω0​ in it, not sin⁡ω0\sin\omega_0sinω0​.
  • Radians, and enough digits. ωc=2πFc/Fs\omega_c = 2\pi F_c/F_sωc​=2πFc​/Fs​ is in radians. With Fc=0.5F_c = 0.5Fc​=0.5 Hz, rounding α\alphaα to 0.99 moves the cut-off to 0.4 Hz, so keep five or six significant figures.
  • Pick the root with ∣α∣<1|\alpha| \lt 1∣α∣<1. The two roots 1±sin⁡ωccos⁡ωc\frac{1 \pm \sin\omega_c}{\cos\omega_c}cosωc​1±sinωc​​ are reciprocals. The plus sign puts the pole outside the unit circle, which makes the causal filter unstable.

Exam-style practice

Each question mixes several sections, the way exam questions tend to. Work through all the parts before opening the answer. For real questions from the Winter 2022–2025 papers, see Past exam questions.

  1. E1 · FIR filter

    A causal FIR filter has h={0.2,0.6,0.2}h = \{0.2, 0.6, 0.2\}h={0.2,0.6,0.2}. (a) Does it have linear phase, and of which type? (b) Find H(ω)H(\omega)H(ω), ∣H(0)∣|H(0)|∣H(0)∣ and ∣H(π)∣|H(\pi)|∣H(π)∣. Is it low-pass or high-pass? (c) What is its group delay? (d) Find the output for x={1,1,1,1}x = \{1, 1, 1, 1\}x={1,1,1,1}. (e) Is it stable?

    Show worked answerHide answer

    (a) Yes: h(0)=h(2)h(0) = h(2)h(0)=h(2) and M=3M = 3M=3 is odd, so it is Type I.

    (b) Factor out the middle: the middle coefficient stands alone and the outer pair gives 2×0.2cos⁡ω2 \times 0.2\cos\omega2×0.2cosω:

    H(ω)=e−jω[0.6+0.4cos⁡ω].H(\omega) = e^{-j\omega}\big[0.6 + 0.4\cos\omega\big].H(ω)=e−jω[0.6+0.4cosω].

    ∣H(0)∣=1|H(0)| = 1∣H(0)∣=1 and ∣H(π)∣=0.2|H(\pi)| = 0.2∣H(π)∣=0.2, so it is low-pass.

    (c) (3−1)/2=1(3-1)/2 = 1(3−1)/2=1 sample.

    (d) y={0.2,0.8,1,1,0.8,0.2}y = \{0.2, 0.8, 1, 1, 0.8, 0.2\}y={0.2,0.8,1,1,0.8,0.2}. Checks: the length is 4+3−1=64 + 3 - 1 = 64+3−1=6, and the sum is 4×1=44 \times 1 = 44×1=4.

    (e) Yes: every FIR filter is stable.

  2. E2 · IIR filter

    An IIR filter is y(n)=0.5 y(n−1)+x(n)y(n) = 0.5\,y(n-1) + x(n)y(n)=0.5y(n−1)+x(n). (a) Find h(n)h(n)h(n). (b) Is it BIBO stable? (c) Find H(ω)H(\omega)H(ω), ∣H(0)∣|H(0)|∣H(0)∣ and ∣H(π)∣|H(\pi)|∣H(π)∣. (d) Could it have linear phase?

    Show worked answerHide answer

    (a) h(n)=0.5n u(n)h(n) = 0.5^n\,u(n)h(n)=0.5nu(n), i.e. 1,0.5,0.25,…1, 0.5, 0.25, \dots1,0.5,0.25,…

    (b) S=1/(1−0.5)=2<∞S = 1/(1 - 0.5) = 2 \lt \inftyS=1/(1−0.5)=2<∞: stable.

    (c) Y(ω)(1−0.5 e−jω)=X(ω)Y(\omega)\big(1 - 0.5\,e^{-j\omega}\big) = X(\omega)Y(ω)(1−0.5e−jω)=X(ω), so

    H(ω)=11−0.5 e−jω,∣H(0)∣=10.5=2,∣H(π)∣=1∣1+0.5∣=0.667.H(\omega) = \frac{1}{1 - 0.5\,e^{-j\omega}}, \qquad |H(0)| = \frac{1}{0.5} = 2, \qquad |H(\pi)| = \frac{1}{|1 + 0.5|} = 0.667.H(ω)=1−0.5e−jω1​,∣H(0)∣=0.51​=2,∣H(π)∣=∣1+0.5∣1​=0.667.

    It is low-pass.

    (d) No. Linear phase needs an impulse response that is symmetric about its middle, and this one starts at n=0n = 0n=0 and never ends, so it has no middle to be symmetric about. That is the IIR price from section 15.

  3. E3 · Sampling meets filtering

    A signal sampled at 8 kHz contains a wanted 500 Hz tone and unwanted 2 kHz interference. (a) Convert both frequencies to ω\omegaω. (b) Does the 8-point moving average remove the interference? (c) What happens to the wanted tone? (d) What delay does the filter add?

    Show worked answerHide answer

    (a) ω=2πF/Fs\omega = 2\pi F/F_sω=2πF/Fs​: 500 Hz gives π/8\pi/8π/8, and 2 kHz gives π/2\pi/2π/2.

    (b) Yes, completely: π/2=2π×2/8\pi/2 = 2\pi \times 2/8π/2=2π×2/8 is one of its zeros.

    (c) It passes with gain ∣H(π/8)∣≈0.64|H(\pi/8)| \approx 0.64∣H(π/8)∣≈0.64: weakened, but not removed. (Check it in the explorer in section 11: 8 taps, ω=0.125π\omega = 0.125\piω=0.125π.)

    (d) The filter is symmetric with 8 taps, so it delays by (8−1)/2=3.5(8-1)/2 = 3.5(8−1)/2=3.5 samples, which is 3.5/8000≈0.443.5/8000 \approx 0.443.5/8000≈0.44 ms.

  4. E4 · Two filters in a row

    Two 3-point averagers, each with h={13,13,13}h = \{\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13\}h={31​,31​,31​}, are connected one after the other. (a) What single impulse response is equivalent? (b) What is its frequency response? (c) What is its group delay? (d) Where is ∣H(ω)∣=0|H(\omega)| = 0∣H(ω)∣=0?

    Show worked answerHide answer

    (a) The second filter multiplies the first one's output spectrum again: Y=H2(H1X)=(H1H2)XY = H_2(H_1X) = (H_1H_2)XY=H2​(H1​X)=(H1​H2​)X. Multiplication in frequency is convolution in time, so the equivalent impulse response is {13,13,13}∗{13,13,13}=19{1,2,3,2,1}\{\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13\} * \{\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13\} = \tfrac19\{1, 2, 3, 2, 1\}{31​,31​,31​}∗{31​,31​,31​}=91​{1,2,3,2,1}.

    (b) The product of the two responses:

    H(ω)=[13 e−jω(1+2cos⁡ω)]2=19 e−j2ω(1+2cos⁡ω)2.H(\omega) = \Big[\tfrac13\,e^{-j\omega}(1 + 2\cos\omega)\Big]^2 = \tfrac19\,e^{-j2\omega}(1 + 2\cos\omega)^2.H(ω)=[31​e−jω(1+2cosω)]2=91​e−j2ω(1+2cosω)2.

    (c) 2 samples: it has 5 symmetric taps, or equally one sample from each stage.

    (d) Where 1+2cos⁡ω=01 + 2\cos\omega = 01+2cosω=0, that is ω=2π/3\omega = 2\pi/3ω=2π/3.

ReviseWinter 2022–2025 papers

Past exam questions

Every paper has four 25-mark questions on the same four themes. Six of the sixteen can already be done: Question 1 in all four years, and Question 2 in 2024 and 2025. All six are worked here.

How the paper works

Length
90 minutes, plus 15 minutes' reading time
Questions
Answer all four. Each is worth 25 marks, split into parts worth between 2 and 13 marks.
Calculator
Non-programmable only
Working
“Marks may be lost if solutions are not shown clearly, or where insufficient workings are shown.”
Equations given
2022: the DTFT, Euler's identities and a window table. 2023: the same, plus the inverse DTFT. 2024 and 2025: the window table only.

Learn these by heart

The last two papers printed only the window table, so don't count on being given the DTFT pair or Euler's identities. On 9 September a student asked whether a formula sheet would be provided, and the lecturer said this year's paper hadn't been written yet. Use the pattern below as a guide; this year's paper may differ.

Ideal band filters, symmetry and phase

Both papers ask the same three things: derive an ideal impulse response with the inverse DTFT (section 12), show that the windowed filter is symmetric (section 16), and find the phase and group delay (sections 17 and 18).

Winter 2022 · Question 125 marks

(a) Starting with the ideal frequency response for a band-pass filter

Hd(ω)={0,−π≤ω<−ωc21,−ωc2≤ω≤−ωc10,−ωc1<ω<ωc11,ωc1≤ω≤ωc20,ωc2<ω≤πH_d(\omega) = \begin{cases} 0, & -\pi \le \omega \lt -\omega_{c2} \\ 1, & -\omega_{c2} \le \omega \le -\omega_{c1} \\ 0, & -\omega_{c1} \lt \omega \lt \omega_{c1} \\ 1, & \omega_{c1} \le \omega \le \omega_{c2} \\ 0, & \omega_{c2} \lt \omega \le \pi \end{cases}Hd​(ω)=⎩⎨⎧​0,1,0,1,0,​−π≤ω<−ωc2​−ωc2​≤ω≤−ωc1​−ωc1​<ω<ωc1​ωc1​≤ω≤ωc2​ωc2​<ω≤π​

derive the ideal impulse response

hd(n)={ωc2−ωc1π,n=0sin⁡(ωc2n)πn−sin⁡(ωc1n)πn,n≠0h_d(n) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\omega_{c2} - \omega_{c1}}{\pi}, & n = 0 \\[10pt] \dfrac{\sin(\omega_{c2}n)}{\pi n} - \dfrac{\sin(\omega_{c1}n)}{\pi n}, & n \ne 0 \end{cases}hd​(n)=⎩⎨⎧​πωc2​−ωc1​​,πnsin(ωc2​n)​−πnsin(ωc1​n)​,​n=0n=0​

[8 marks]

Show worked answerHide answer

Use the inverse DTFT, as for the ideal low-pass in section 12. Hd(ω)H_d(\omega)Hd​(ω) is 1 on two bands and 0 elsewhere, so the integral splits in two:

hd(n)=12π∫−ππHd(ω) ejωn dω=12π[∫−ωc2−ωc1ejωn dω+∫ωc1ωc2ejωn dω].\begin{aligned} h_d(n) &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} H_d(\omega)\,e^{j\omega n}\,d\omega \\[4pt] &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\int_{-\omega_{c2}}^{-\omega_{c1}} e^{j\omega n}\,d\omega + \int_{\omega_{c1}}^{\omega_{c2}} e^{j\omega n}\,d\omega\right]. \end{aligned}hd​(n)​=2π1​∫−ππ​Hd​(ω)ejωndω=2π1​[∫−ωc2​−ωc1​​ejωndω+∫ωc1​ωc2​​ejωndω].​

n=0n = 0n=0: the integrand is 1, so each integral is the width of its band: hd(0)=12π⋅2(ωc2−ωc1)=ωc2−ωc1πh_d(0) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot 2(\omega_{c2} - \omega_{c1}) = \frac{\omega_{c2} - \omega_{c1}}{\pi}hd​(0)=2π1​⋅2(ωc2​−ωc1​)=πωc2​−ωc1​​.

n≠0n \ne 0n=0: integrate, then pair the terms at ±ωc2\pm\omega_{c2}±ωc2​ and at ±ωc1\pm\omega_{c1}±ωc1​ with Euler's identity:

hd(n)=(e−jωc1n−e−jωc2n)+(ejωc2n−ejωc1n)2πjn=2jsin⁡(ωc2n)−2jsin⁡(ωc1n)2πjn=sin⁡(ωc2n)−sin⁡(ωc1n)πn.\begin{aligned} h_d(n) &= \frac{\big(e^{-j\omega_{c1}n} - e^{-j\omega_{c2}n}\big) + \big(e^{j\omega_{c2}n} - e^{j\omega_{c1}n}\big)}{2\pi jn} \\[4pt] &= \frac{2j\sin(\omega_{c2}n) - 2j\sin(\omega_{c1}n)}{2\pi jn} = \frac{\sin(\omega_{c2}n) - \sin(\omega_{c1}n)}{\pi n}. \end{aligned}hd​(n)​=2πjn(e−jωc1​n−e−jωc2​n)+(ejωc2​n−ejωc1​n)​=2πjn2jsin(ωc2​n)−2jsin(ωc1​n)​=πnsin(ωc2​n)−sin(ωc1​n)​.​

A quick check: a band-pass is a wide low-pass minus a narrow one, Hd=HLP(ωc2)−HLP(ωc1)H_d = H_{LP}(\omega_{c2}) - H_{LP}(\omega_{c1})Hd​=HLP​(ωc2​)−HLP​(ωc1​), so hd(n)h_d(n)hd​(n) is the difference of two section 12 sincs. Both cases agree with that.

For the marks. Set up the integral with the right limits, treat n=0n = 0n=0 separately, and show the Euler step.

(b) A FIR band-pass filter designed using the rectangular window has the impulse response

h(n)={sin⁡ ⁣(ωc2(n−M−12))π(n−M−12)−sin⁡ ⁣(ωc1(n−M−12))π(n−M−12),0≤n≤M−1, n≠M−12ωc2−ωc1π,n=M−12 for M odd0,n<0, n>M−1h(n) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sin\!\big(\omega_{c2}(n - \frac{M-1}{2})\big)}{\pi(n - \frac{M-1}{2})} - \dfrac{\sin\!\big(\omega_{c1}(n - \frac{M-1}{2})\big)}{\pi(n - \frac{M-1}{2})}, & 0 \le n \le M-1,\ n \ne \frac{M-1}{2} \\[12pt] \dfrac{\omega_{c2} - \omega_{c1}}{\pi}, & n = \frac{M-1}{2}\ \text{for } M \text{ odd} \\[8pt] 0, & n \lt 0,\ n \gt M-1 \end{cases}h(n)=⎩⎨⎧​π(n−2M−1​)sin(ωc2​(n−2M−1​))​−π(n−2M−1​)sin(ωc1​(n−2M−1​))​,πωc2​−ωc1​​,0,​0≤n≤M−1, n=2M−1​n=2M−1​ for M oddn<0, n>M−1​

With MMM odd, show that the filter coefficients have positive symmetry, h(n)=h(M−1−n)h(n) = h(M-1-n)h(n)=h(M−1−n).

[8 marks]

Show worked answerHide answer

Let c=M−12c = \frac{M-1}{2}c=2M−1​, a whole number because MMM is odd. Inside 0≤n≤M−10 \le n \le M-10≤n≤M−1 the filter is the ideal response shifted right by ccc and cut to MMM samples: h(n)=hd(n−c)h(n) = h_d(n - c)h(n)=hd​(n−c), where m=n−cm = n - cm=n−c is the distance from the middle.

The mirror image of nnn is M−1−nM - 1 - nM−1−n. Its distance from the middle is (M−1−n)−c=c−n=−m(M - 1 - n) - c = c - n = -m(M−1−n)−c=c−n=−m, so h(M−1−n)=hd(−m)h(M-1-n) = h_d(-m)h(M−1−n)=hd​(−m).

Now hdh_dhd​ is even. Sine is odd, and the denominator changes sign too:

hd(−m)=sin⁡(−ωc2m)−sin⁡(−ωc1m)π(−m)=−[sin⁡(ωc2m)−sin⁡(ωc1m)]−πm=hd(m).h_d(-m) = \frac{\sin(-\omega_{c2}m) - \sin(-\omega_{c1}m)}{\pi(-m)} = \frac{-\big[\sin(\omega_{c2}m) - \sin(\omega_{c1}m)\big]}{-\pi m} = h_d(m).hd​(−m)=π(−m)sin(−ωc2​m)−sin(−ωc1​m)​=−πm−[sin(ωc2​m)−sin(ωc1​m)]​=hd​(m).

So h(M−1−n)=hd(−m)=hd(m)=h(n)h(M-1-n) = h_d(-m) = h_d(m) = h(n)h(M−1−n)=hd​(−m)=hd​(m)=h(n). The middle sample n=cn = cn=c is its own mirror image, and outside 0≤n≤M−10 \le n \le M-10≤n≤M−1 both sides are zero, because n<0n \lt 0n<0 exactly when M−1−n>M−1M-1-n \gt M-1M−1−n>M−1. Hence h(n)=h(M−1−n)h(n) = h(M-1-n)h(n)=h(M−1−n) for every nnn: positive symmetry, a Type I filter (section 16).

(c) For a FIR filter with M=5M = 5M=5 and coefficients with positive symmetry, determine the phase response and the group delay of the filter.

[9 marks]

Show worked answerHide answer

With M=5M = 5M=5: h(0)=h(4)h(0) = h(4)h(0)=h(4) and h(1)=h(3)h(1) = h(3)h(1)=h(3), and h(2)h(2)h(2) is the unpaired middle.

H(ω)=∑n=04h(n) e−jωn=h(0)+h(1)e−jω+h(2)e−j2ω+h(1)e−j3ω+h(0)e−j4ω.\begin{aligned} H(\omega) &= \sum_{n=0}^{4} h(n)\,e^{-j\omega n} \\[4pt] &= h(0) + h(1)e^{-j\omega} + h(2)e^{-j2\omega} + h(1)e^{-j3\omega} + h(0)e^{-j4\omega}. \end{aligned}H(ω)​=n=0∑4​h(n)e−jωn=h(0)+h(1)e−jω+h(2)e−j2ω+h(1)e−j3ω+h(0)e−j4ω.​

Factor out the middle term's exponential, e−j2ωe^{-j2\omega}e−j2ω, and pair the terms with Euler:

H(ω)=e−j2ω[h(0)(ej2ω+e−j2ω)+h(1)(ejω+e−jω)+h(2)]=e−j2ω [h(2)+2h(1)cos⁡ω+2h(0)cos⁡2ω]⏟A(ω), real.\begin{aligned} H(\omega) &= e^{-j2\omega}\Big[h(0)\big(e^{j2\omega} + e^{-j2\omega}\big) + h(1)\big(e^{j\omega} + e^{-j\omega}\big) + h(2)\Big] \\[4pt] &= e^{-j2\omega}\,\underbrace{\big[h(2) + 2h(1)\cos\omega + 2h(0)\cos 2\omega\big]}_{A(\omega),\ \text{real}}. \end{aligned}H(ω)​=e−j2ω[h(0)(ej2ω+e−j2ω)+h(1)(ejω+e−jω)+h(2)]=e−j2ωA(ω), real[h(2)+2h(1)cosω+2h(0)cos2ω]​​.​

A(ω)A(\omega)A(ω) is real because the coefficients and the cosines are real. The phase is therefore

θ(ω)={−2ω,A(ω)>0−2ω+π,A(ω)<0\theta(\omega) = \begin{cases} -2\omega, & A(\omega) \gt 0 \\ -2\omega + \pi, & A(\omega) \lt 0 \end{cases}θ(ω)={−2ω,−2ω+π,​A(ω)>0A(ω)<0​

a straight line of slope −M−12=−2-\frac{M-1}{2} = -2−2M−1​=−2, with jumps of π\piπ wherever A(ω)A(\omega)A(ω) changes sign: linear phase with α=2\alpha = 2α=2 and β=0\beta = 0β=0.

The group delay is Tg(ω)=−dθdω=2T_g(\omega) = -\dfrac{d\theta}{d\omega} = 2Tg​(ω)=−dωdθ​=2 samples at every frequency. The π\piπ jumps don't count, because they are sign flips rather than delays (section 17).

(a) Starting with the ideal frequency response for a band-stop filter

Hd(ω)={1,−π≤ω<−ωc20,−ωc2≤ω≤−ωc11,−ωc1<ω<ωc10,ωc1≤ω≤ωc21,ωc2<ω≤πH_d(\omega) = \begin{cases} 1, & -\pi \le \omega \lt -\omega_{c2} \\ 0, & -\omega_{c2} \le \omega \le -\omega_{c1} \\ 1, & -\omega_{c1} \lt \omega \lt \omega_{c1} \\ 0, & \omega_{c1} \le \omega \le \omega_{c2} \\ 1, & \omega_{c2} \lt \omega \le \pi \end{cases}Hd​(ω)=⎩⎨⎧​1,0,1,0,1,​−π≤ω<−ωc2​−ωc2​≤ω≤−ωc1​−ωc1​<ω<ωc1​ωc1​≤ω≤ωc2​ωc2​<ω≤π​

derive the ideal impulse response

hd(n)=(e−jωc2n−e−jπn)+(ejωc1n−e−jωc1n)+(ejπn−ejωc2n)2πjn=2jsin⁡(ωc1n)−2jsin⁡(ωc2n)+2jsin⁡(πn)2πjn.\begin{aligned} h_d(n) &= \frac{\big(e^{-j\omega_{c2}n} - e^{-j\pi n}\big) + \big(e^{j\omega_{c1}n} - e^{-j\omega_{c1}n}\big) + \big(e^{j\pi n} - e^{j\omega_{c2}n}\big)}{2\pi jn} \\[4pt] &= \frac{2j\sin(\omega_{c1}n) - 2j\sin(\omega_{c2}n) + 2j\sin(\pi n)}{2\pi jn}. \end{aligned}hd​(n)​=2πjn(e−jωc2​n−e−jπn)+(ejωc1​n−e−jωc1​n)+(ejπn−ejωc2​n)​=2πjn2jsin(ωc1​n)−2jsin(ωc2​n)+2jsin(πn)​.​

It starts at 0 at DC (the zero at z=1z = 1z=1), passes through 12\tfrac1221​ at Fc=0.5F_c = 0.5Fc​=0.5 Hz, and levels off at 1: it is 0.8 at 1 Hz, 0.99 at 5 Hz and exactly 1 at Fs/2=125F_s/2 = 125Fs​/2=125 Hz. The first 5 Hz

For a cut-off this low, the response is very close to an analogue first-order high-pass, ∣H∣2≈F2F2+Fc2|H|^2 \approx \dfrac{F^2}{F^2 + F_c^2}∣H∣2≈F2+Fc2​F2​. That is where 0.2 at Fc/2F_c/2Fc​/2 and 0.8 at 2Fc2F_c2Fc​ come from.

(f) Draw the pole-zero plot of the transfer function HHP(z)H_{HP}(z)HHP​(z) of part (b).

[4 marks]

Show worked answerHide answer

Multiply top and bottom by zzz: HHP(z)=0.993756 z−1z−0.987512H_{HP}(z) = 0.993756\,\dfrac{z - 1}{z - 0.987512}HHP​(z)=0.993756z−0.987512z−1​. There is one zero, at z=1z = 1z=1 on the unit circle, and one pole, at z=0.987512z = 0.987512z=0.987512 on the real axis just inside it. The filter is causal, so its ROC is ∣z∣>0.987512|z| \gt 0.987512∣z∣>0.987512, which contains the unit circle: the filter is stable.

The zero at z=1z = 1z=1 blocks DC. Because the pole sits just behind it, moving even a little way round the circle from z=1z = 1z=1 makes the distances to the pole and to the zero almost equal, so the gain climbs back to 1 very quickly. The closer the pole is to the zero, the lower the cut-off (Z-Transform slides 45–47, still to come).

Still to come

The lectures of 22 and 23 September covered Z-Transform slides 1–23, with a first look at stability. The rest of that slide set, in order; each part joins Part 2 when the lectures reach it.

Slides 24–26
The system function. Take the z-transform of a difference equation term by term to get H(z)=Y(z)/X(z)H(z) = Y(z)/X(z)H(z)=Y(z)/X(z). An FIR filter is an all-zero system; an IIR filter has poles as well.
Slides 27–28
IIR filters. The difference equation and the impulse response are two views of one filter: y(n)=a y(n−1)+x(n)y(n) = a\,y(n-1) + x(n)y(n)=ay(n−1)+x(n) has h(n)=anu(n)h(n) = a^n u(n)h(n)=anu(n).
Slides 29–31
Where the pole sits decides the behaviour. A single real pole at 12\tfrac1221​ decays, at −1-1−1 it alternates without growing, and at −1.1-1.1−1.1 it alternates and grows.
Slides 32–36
Stability, with a worked example: the poles of 1/(1−12z−1+516z−2)1/(1 - \tfrac12 z^{-1} + \tfrac{5}{16}z^{-2})1/(1−21​z−1+165​z−2) are 14±12j\tfrac14 \pm \tfrac12 j41​±21​j, both inside the unit circle. Section 31 already covers it (Q31.2).
Slides 37–44
The frequency response from H(z)H(z)H(z). Magnitude as a product of distances to the zeros over distances to the poles, phase as a sum of angles, worked for (1+z−1)/(1−0.7071z−1)(1 + z^{-1})/(1 - 0.7071z^{-1})(1+z−1)/(1−0.7071z−1).
Slides 45–47
Reading the response off the pole-zero plot. The gain rises near a pole and falls near a zero; poles and zeros at the origin change only the phase.
Slides 48–53
Two FIR examples. The 5-point moving average has its zeros on the unit circle at 0.4π0.4\pi0.4π, 0.8π0.8\pi0.8π, 1.2π1.2\pi1.2π and 1.6π1.6\pi1.6π. A 9-tap windowed filter has six zeros on the circle and a reciprocal pair at 0.442 and 2.264.
